meta.title: El Niño 2026–27 research
meta.intro: The most useful current reports and studies on the 2026–27 El Niño: forecasting, impacts, anticipatory action, response and finance. Each entry says why it is worth reading, gives its key numbers, and links to the problems on the map it informs.
meta.method: Checked means the numbers were verified against the source page itself. For the long WHO and FEWS NET reports, roughly the first 40% of the text was checked word for word and the rest from a summary. Found means the source was located by search but not read in full; treat its description as a pointer, not a claim. Compiled by Claude for this project on 6 November 2026.

themes.name: Forecasting and monitoring
themes.note: Where the strength and timing numbers come from, and how far to trust them.

themes.name: Food security and impacts
themes.note: Where and when harvests, prices and people will be hit. The main point: impacts stretch into 2027–28.

themes.name: Health
themes.note: El Niño does not cause disease directly. It modifies risk (WHO's framing).

themes.name: Anticipatory action
themes.note: What is launched before the shock, on which triggers, and what the last cycle showed.

themes.name: Finance and response
themes.note: How much money, from where, and how late. Plus macroeconomics.

themes.name: Foundations
themes.note: Classic studies that most of the reports above cite.

takeaways.title: The peak is now, hunger comes later
takeaways.text: The anomaly peaks at the end of 2026, but the worst food-security outcomes come in 2027: March–August 2027 in unimodal East Africa, the November 2027 – March 2028 lean season in Southern Africa (FEWS NET).

takeaways.title: No analogue
takeaways.text: WMO forecasts up to +3.8 °C, beyond anything in its 40-year monitoring record. Triggers calibrated on 1997/98 and 2015/16 may misfire.

takeaways.title: Money for early action exists, but it is thin
takeaways.text: The FAO–WFP joint appeal asks $202M for 8.8 million people, and CERF is ready to release up to $100M. UNICEF says less than 1% of international humanitarian aid is available for anticipatory action.

gaps.text: Independent evaluations of the 2026 activations. So far there are only launch announcements. The nearest evidence is WFP's 2023/24 Southern Africa review and the ENAAR after-action review.
Methods for triggers when there is no historical analogue. The Welthungerhilfe briefing warns against using ENSO or IOD as stand-alone triggers, but no method exists for a record event.
A summary of sovereign risk insurance for this season. Only the 2024 ARC payouts are documented; nothing found on 2026–27 coverage or payouts from ARC, CCRIF or PCRIC.
Migration and conflict. Almost no recent empirical work; only an unreviewed preprint.

items.title: WMO Global Seasonal Climate Outlook informs humanitarian action
items.why: The latest official estimate of strength and regional signals. This is the source of the 'up to +3.8 °C' figure for November–January.
facts: Tropical Pacific anomaly up to +3.8 °C in Nov 2026 – Jan 2027; WMO Secretary-General Saulo: 'literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades'
East Africa wetter than normal in the Oct–Dec rains; Southern Africa drier from November
Southeast Asia: heat, rainfall deficits, wildfire and haze; Central America, southern Caribbean and Amazon: higher drought risk

items.title: El Niño/La Niña Update (August 2026)
items.why: The official periodic bulletin: confirms the event is established and gives seasonal probabilities.
facts: By mid-August El Niño had 'become firmly established'
Nearly 100% probability it persists through Sep–Nov and Dec–Feb
Expected to reach very strong intensity, peaking towards the end of the year

items.title: How confident should we be in a prediction of El Niño?
items.why: The best short explanation of the spring predictability barrier and model spread. A good case study of why April–May decisions were made under real uncertainty.
facts: April ECMWF ensemble members gave September Niño-3.4 anomalies from about +1.7 to +3.3 °C; the C3S multi-system ensemble from +0.2 to +3.3 °C
March 2017 is named the worst March ENSO forecast in SEAS5's record
Advice: confidence arrives around late May to June

items.title: ENSO Diagnostic Discussion (monthly)
items.why: The primary source behind figures quoted by FEWS NET, PAHO and the press: the new RONI index and the probability of a very strong event.
facts: Per secondary sources: RONI for Jul–Sep +1.7 °C, expected peak at or above +2.5 °C, greater than 90% chance of a very strong event through the 2026/27 northern autumn and winter

items.title: El Niño Outlook
items.why: A forecast centre independent of NOAA and ECMWF. Useful for the 'different sources, different signals' problem.

items.title: 2026–2027 El Niño food security impacts (Special Report)
items.why: The key document on timing. It shows hunger arriving 6–18 months after the rains fail and breaks this down by region. First of a series of three; the next is due late 2026.
facts: Index at or above +2 °C in September; only seven very strong events since 1950, closest analogue 1997/98
Unimodal East Africa: food insecurity most severe March–August 2027 (Ethiopia, South Sudan, Sudan, Karamoja)
Southern Africa: most severe in the November 2027 – March 2028 lean season
Bimodal East Africa: rains at or above 150% of average in many areas, flood risk highest along the Shabelle and Juba; a risk of Famine (IPC 5) in southern Somalia, though not the most likely scenario
Global cereal output fell at most 3.9% in strong El Niño years since 1980; USDA projects −2.7% for 2026/27

items.title: How This Year's Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
items.why: A fresh feature that ties together climate, harvests, fisheries and shrinking aid budgets.
facts: WFP: an additional 49 million people in acute food insecurity by end of 2027 (274 million total)
October anomaly +3.5 °C against a previous record of about 2.75 °C
Global aid funds in 2025 were 30% below their 2022 peak; in Somalia WFP reached 10 million people in 2022 and can now afford fewer than one million
Peru's anchovy season closed early; global fishmeal output about half of last year's

items.title: Strengthening 2026 El Niño: Potential Implications (Briefing Note)
items.why: The most practical operational briefing: region by region, with concrete advice for people designing triggers.
facts: Somalia (FAO-SWALIM): 71 strategic water sources at very high risk, 524 at high risk
Central America: more than 70% probability of below-normal Oct–Dec rainfall
Recommendation: 'Do not use ENSO or IOD as stand-alone triggers'

items.title: Southern Africa Food Security Outlook, June 2026
items.why: Regional detail for Southern Africa: an early lean season compounded by El Niño.

items.title: Emerging 2026 El Niño (June briefing)
items.why: The earlier version of the WHH briefing. Useful to see how assessments shifted between June and October.

items.title: Global Public Health Situation Analysis: El Niño 2026
items.who: WHO Health Emergencies Programme (with IASC ENSO Cell, MSF, WMO)
items.why: The only global health risk analysis by disease and region. Sets the frame of El Niño as a risk modifier.
facts: Malnutrition rated 'very high risk' (likelihood 'almost certain'); cholera and other waterborne diseases also 'very high'
Regions: Southern Africa (drought Oct 2026 – Mar 2027), Central America's Dry Corridor (heat and CKDu), South and Southeast Asia
Priority: keep essential services running (maternal and child health, immunisation, NCD care, mental health)

items.title: Strengthening El Niño raises growing health risks across the Americas (with Situation Report 1)
items.why: The only region with regular monitoring of health impacts already running. A good model for the map's data.
facts: More than 5.2 million people affected or at risk; 8 countries or territories have declared emergencies or alerts
Peru: at least 70 deaths and more than 600 health facilities affected (Dec 2025 – Aug 2026)
Colombia: wildfires, heavy rain, an active dengue outbreak, malaria and yellow fever risks

items.title: Monitoring El Niño, Report 1 (PDF)
items.why: Full text of the situation report behind the press release above.

items.title: El Niño 2026–2027: seizing the moment
items.who: Anticipation Hub with the AA Task Force (FAO, IFRC, OCHA, Climate Centre, Start Network, WHH, WFP)
items.why: The joint position of the anticipatory action community for this cycle, with return-on-investment figures. The best entry point to the topic.
facts: By June 2026, frameworks activated in Central America, East Africa and the Sahel: over $35M for almost 2 million people
Anticipatory action frameworks exist in 75 countries
Returns: Horn of Africa $1 → $2.3–3.3 net benefit; Southern Africa 2023/24 a 30% net benefit, $1 early = $1.3 later

items.title: Anticipating the impact of drought in southern African countries: key findings from the 2023/24 activations
items.why: The main body of evidence from the last El Niño: what was done and what it achieved. Rely on it until 2026 evaluations exist.
facts: The largest anticipatory action activation in Southern Africa to date: Lesotho, Madagascar, Mozambique, Zimbabwe
Drought forecasts issued in July 2023, before planting
$14M of pre-arranged finance; over 1.2 million people received early warnings

items.title: Red Cross activates Early Action Protocols at the first signs of drought in El Salvador, Guatemala and Colombia
items.why: A concrete example of a staged trigger (money released in tranches as thresholds are reached) and of national met services' role.
facts: CHF 1.2M from the DREF, released in stages; more than 22,000 people
Triggers from national services: INSIVUMEH 70%, IDEAM more than 50% probability of below-normal rain
Only $1 in every $10 of humanitarian funding goes to risk reduction

items.title: Southern Africa El Niño Anticipation After Action Review (ENAAR)
items.why: Review of 2023/24: trigger model performance, cost-effectiveness, government recommitments. Worth requesting the materials if they are not public.
facts: Topics: performance of forecast-based trigger models, return on investment of ex-ante operations, high-level recommitment from directors of national agencies

items.title: El Niño 2026–27: 'No excuse for inaction'
items.who: Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre
items.why: The Climate Centre's position on this event. The site did not load during checking.

items.title: El Niño 2026: a closing window for anticipatory action in Latin America and the Caribbean
items.why: Regional analysis of the window to act in Latin America and the Caribbean. Could not be read.

items.title: From forecast to risk: an anticipatory analysis of the 2026–27 El Niño
items.why: Directly about the forecast-to-risk gap, but an unreviewed preprint that could not be read. Check the authors before citing.

items.title: OCHA El Niño 2026 presentation
items.why: How OCHA plans collective frameworks and CERF for this cycle.

items.title: Bracing for El Niño: FAO and WFP launch joint appeal to protect 8.8 million people
items.why: The first-ever joint FAO–WFP anticipatory action appeal, and the basis for problem 3.2. Full appeal: openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/ce0220en.
facts: $202M to protect 8.8 million people in 22 countries; 1.2 million already covered, $167M needed for a further 7.6 million
'Every dollar invested in anticipatory response can result in up to $7 in avoided losses and response costs'
Measures: cash, seeds, livestock protection, water, flood protection, agricultural advisories

items.title: UN readies US$100 million as stronger El Niño threatens millions
items.why: Records the CERF envelope for this cycle. Per Weather.com on 22 October, more than $50M had been released to 11 countries by then.
facts: CERF ready to disburse up to $100M
More than $20M already allocated for anticipatory action in six countries

items.title: 162 million children in Eastern and Southern Africa exposed to El Niño (UNICEF figures)
items.why: The key figure on how little goes to anticipatory action. The UNICEF original is worth finding.
facts: More than 162 million children in 13 countries live in exposed areas
Less than 1% of international humanitarian assistance is available for anticipatory action
UNICEF seeks $173M within its existing 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children requirements

items.title: UNICEF LAC Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1 (El Niño Multi-Country Preparedness and Response)
items.why: The first multi-country situation report on the response in Latin America and the Caribbean.

items.title: Start Fund Risk Bulletin, August 2026
items.why: An NGO pooled fund's view of risk. Relevant to fragmented pooled funds.

items.title: Super El Niño risk: more inflation in Asia, oversupply in Latin America yet little disruption in financial markets
items.why: The best of the market notes: inflation by country and commodity, with historical losses.
facts: IMF: a typical El Niño raises global food prices by around 5% within a year
Indonesia most exposed (+2.3pp inflation), Malaysia and the Philippines most insulated (+0.7pp)
Highest price risk: sugar, palm oil and rice

items.title: ASEAN and India: El Niño exposure
items.why: A bank's country-by-country exposure analysis for Asia.

items.title: African Risk Capacity expects parametric drought insurance to trigger for four countries
items.why: The 2024 precedent: parametric insurance payouts after El Niño. A baseline for basis risk and insurance coverage.

items.title: Persistent effect of El Niño on global economic growth
items.why: The main study of long-lasting economic losses. Its figures of $4.1 trillion (1982–83) and $5.7 trillion (1997–98) are cited by Allianz and many others.
facts: GDP losses persist for years after an event; tropical countries lose the most

items.title: Civil conflicts are associated with the global climate
items.why: The classic study linking ENSO to civil conflict risk in the tropics. Hard to discuss problems 9.2 and 6.10 without it.
facts: The probability of new civil conflicts in tropical countries roughly doubles in El Niño years compared with La Niña years
